catalog_quote: Stress in Gayo is predictable and therefore non-phonemic. Stress is characterised by higher pitch and longer duration than unstressed syllables. Gayo has moraic iambic stress, i.e. primary word stress falls on the final syllable of the word; stress is shifting when suffixes are added. In this section, primary stress is indicated by a raised stress mark ( ˈ) preceding the syllable. Secondary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, i.e. the syllable preceding the syllable bearing primary stress, and is indicated by a lowered stress mark ( ˌ): anak [ˌaˈnãk] 'offspring' asu [ˌaˈsu:] 'dog' siut [ˌsɪˈʊt] 'burn' rëje [ˌrɤ:ˈdʒɤ:] 'king' iô [ˌɪˈjo:] 'afternoon' petukel [pəˌtʊˈkəl] 'pumpkin' i-pet-inum-en [ɪpətɪˌnʊˈmə̃n] 'give water (to an animal)' Reduplicated forms (§3.5) have double-word stress ... 2.2.1.2 Phrase stress. sources.quote: 'In Gayo stress is apparently non-contrastive ... In isolation stress normally occurs on the final syllable of the word, e.g. asu [a"su:] 'dog' ... The correlates of stress are increased vowel duration, loudness and pitch. ... in practice the appearance of the three correlates is not restricted to the stressed final syllable, and it is perhaps better to describe them as occurring variably over a two syllable window (except where the pre-final syllable is open and contains /ə/). sources.locator: section 'Stress placement', pp.112-113 (PDF pp.6-7); transcription note p.114
sources.note: Same author plus a phonetician, one year after the grammar: restates final stress in isolation but describes the correlates as spread over a final two-syllable window, often heard as penultimate in connected speech, obligatorily final after an open schwa penult, and not always shifting onto -ni; this both qualifies our 'fixed final, no weight condition' reading of Eades 2005 and largely explains the Hazeu 1907 'penult unless schwa' conflict the record carries.
